html:
The moment in 1696 when the Dutch East India Company brought coffee seedlings from Malabar in south India to Batavia on Java. The first plants were lost to a flood, and a second shipment in 1699 took root.

Until then nearly all the world's coffee came from Yemen through the port of Mocha, after coffee reached Yemen from Ethiopia. The Dutch wanted their own supply. By 1711 Java was shipping coffee to Amsterdam, and within a few decades Dutch Java coffee was competing with Mocha on European markets, which is why "java" became slang for coffee.

The crop was grown by Javanese farmers under heavy pressure, first through forced deliveries to the Company and later under the Cultivation System of the 1830s. In the late 19th century leaf rust, the disease that also ended coffee in Ceylon, wrecked many Arabica estates, and planters switched to hardier robusta. See also Coffee in Java.
